case_info.scenario: A woman in her 60s presented with a 2-year history of painful pink vesicular and papular lesions on the vulva and thighs. The patient had undergone hysterectomy, adnexectomy, and concurrent chemoradiotherapy for cervical cancer 8 years prior to the visit. She had a 7-year history of hypertension but no sexually transmitted infections or other systemic diseases. Physical examination revealed scattered or clustered pink translucent vesicles and papules in the bilateral labia majora and inner thigh (Figure 1A). The lesions were soft to moderately firm in texture and contained clear fluid. No enlargement of the inguinal lymph nodes was detected on palpation. Results of pelvic magnetic resonance imaging and abdominal computed tomography revealed no abnormalities. A histopathological biopsy was performed (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, Clinical image showing vesicular and papular lesions on the vulva and thighs. B, Multiple dilated lymphatic channels containing proteinaceous fluid in the superficial dermis, lined by a flat endothelium.
case_info.explanation: Histopathological examination revealed multiple dilated lymphatic channels containing proteinaceous fluid in the superficial dermis, lined by a flat endothelium (Figure 1B). Immunohistochemical staining was positive for D2-40 in endothelial cells (Figure 2). A diagnosis of acquired vulvar lymphangioma (AVL) was made. AVL, also known as acquired lymphangiectasia of the vulva, is a rare, benign condition associated with architectural disruption, obstruction, and further dilation of previously normal lymphatic channels. It can occur secondary to cancers, trauma, radiotherapy, surgery, infections, and inflammatory diseases.1,2Cervical carcinoma, especially cervical squamous cell carcinoma, is the most common AVL-associated cancer.3Clinically, AVL presents as skin-colored papules or translucent, reddish vesicles, which may be scattered or clustered in a frog-spawn pattern on the vulvar region. Lesions may be asymptomatic or associated with pruritus, burning sensations, serous fluid leakage, or secondary infections. Histopathologically, AVL is characterized by dilated lymphatic channels lined with flat endothelial cells. Additional features include varying degrees of papillomatous changes in the epidermis, hyperkeratosis, acanthosis, and erosion. Immunohistochemistry staining with lymphatic markers such as D2-40 can help to confirm the nature of the vessels as being of lymphatic origin.4Treatment is challenging because of the high recurrence rate, with an overall recurrence rate of approximately 43% after initial treatment.1Surgical excision is the most common treatment, with postsurgical recurrence rates of 23.1% to 25%; complete excision of skin, including lymphatic cisterns in subcutaneous tissue, may prevent recurrence.5,6Other treatments include sclerotherapy, laser therapy, cryotherapy, electrocautery, radiotherapy, or photodynamic therapy.2The present patient was referred to the gynecology department for surgical resection of the vulvar lesions; however, the procedure was postponed due to the sudden onset of acute lower extremity lymphangitis. Although the condition improved after anti-inflammatory therapy, the patient refused further treatment and was lost to follow-up. Differential diagnoses in the present case include syringoma, molluscum contagiosum, and condyloma acuminatum. Molluscum contagiosum, caused by the molluscum contagiosum virus, is clinically characterized by asymptomatic, small, shiny, dome-shaped papules with central umbilication. Large cells with granular, eosinophilic, intracytoplasmic molluscum bodies are a typical histopathological feature.7Vulvar syringomas are benign adnexal tumors typically characterized by multiple small, firm, skin-colored to light brown papules scattered on the labia majora. These lesions are usually asymptomatic or present with pruritus or pain. Histopathological examination reveals nests of eccrine ducts and tadpolelike structures embedded in fibrous stroma.8Condylomata acuminata, or genital warts, is a common sexually transmitted infection caused by the human papillomavirus. Lesions may manifest in various forms, including smooth, flat, keratotic papules or exophytic cauliflowerlike masses. Koilocytic change is a helpful histopathological feature of condylomata acuminata and serves as a critical clue for differential diagnosis.9 This patient’s presentation illustrates findings typical of AVL, an uncommon complication from patients with a history of cervical cancer, radiation therapy, or surgical intervention. AVL should be considered in the differential diagnosis when papular or vesicular lesions develop in the vulvar region.

case_info.explanation: Histopathological examination revealed multiple dilated lymphatic channels containing proteinaceous fluid in the superficial dermis, lined by a flat endothelium (Figure 1B). Immunohistochemical staining was positive for D2-40 in endothelial cells (Figure 2). A diagnosis of acquired vulvar lymphangioma (AVL) was made. AVL, also known as acquired lymphangiectasia of the vulva, is a rare, benign condition associated with architectural disruption, obstruction, and further dilation of previously normal lymphatic channels. It can occur secondary to cancers, trauma, radiotherapy, surgery, infections, and inflammatory diseases.1,2Cervical carcinoma, especially cervical squamous cell carcinoma, is the most common AVL-associated cancer.3Clinically, AVL presents as skin-colored papules or translucent, reddish vesicles, which may be scattered or clustered in a frog-spawn pattern on the vulvar region. Lesions may be asymptomatic or associated with pruritus, burning sensations, serous fluid leakage, or secondary infections. Histopathologically, AVL is characterized by dilated lymphatic channels lined with flat endothelial cells. Additional features include varying degrees of papillomatous changes in the epidermis, hyperkeratosis, acanthosis, and erosion. Immunohistochemistry staining with lymphatic markers such as D2-40 can help to confirm the nature of the vessels as being of lymphatic origin.4Treatment is challenging because of the high recurrence rate, with an overall recurrence rate of approximately 43% after initial treatment.1Surgical excision is the most common treatment, with postsurgical recurrence rates of 23.1% to 25%; complete excision of skin, including lymphatic cisterns in subcutaneous tissue, may prevent recurrence.5,6Other treatments include sclerotherapy, laser therapy, cryotherapy, electrocautery, radiotherapy, or photodynamic therapy.2The present patient was referred to the gynecology department for surgical resection of the vulvar lesions; however, the procedure was postponed due to the sudden onset of acute lower extremity lymphangitis. Although the condition improved after anti-inflammatory therapy, the patient refused further treatment and was lost to follow-up. Differential diagnoses in the present case include syringoma, molluscum contagiosum, and condyloma acuminatum. Molluscum contagiosum, caused by the molluscum contagiosum virus, is clinically characterized by asymptomatic, small, shiny, dome-shaped papules with central umbilication. Large cells with granular, eosinophilic, intracytoplasmic molluscum bodies are a typical histopathological feature.7Vulvar syringomas are benign adnexal tumors typically characterized by multiple small, firm, skin-colored to light brown papules scattered on the labia majora. These lesions are usually asymptomatic or present with pruritus or pain. Histopathological examination reveals nests of eccrine ducts and tadpolelike structures embedded in fibrous stroma.8Condylomata acuminata, or genital warts, is a common sexually transmitted infection caused by the human papillomavirus. Lesions may manifest in various forms, including smooth, flat, keratotic papules or exophytic cauliflowerlike masses. Koilocytic change is a helpful histopathological feature of condylomata acuminata and serves as a critical clue for differential diagnosis.9 This patient’s presentation illustrates findings typical of AVL, an uncommon complication from patients with a history of cervical cancer, radiation therapy, or surgical intervention. AVL should be considered in the differential diagnosis when papular or vesicular lesions develop in the vulvar region.

Immunohistochemical staining was positive for D2-40 in endothelial cells (Figure 2). A diagnosis of acquired vulvar lymphangioma (AVL) was made. AVL, also known as acquired lymphangiectasia of the vulva, is a rare, benign condition associated with architectural disruption, obstruction, and further dilation of previously normal lymphatic channels. It can occur secondary to cancers, trauma, radiotherapy, surgery, infections, and inflammatory diseases.1,2Cervical carcinoma, especially cervical squamous cell carcinoma, is the most common AVL-associated cancer.3Clinically, AVL presents as skin-colored papules or translucent, reddish vesicles, which may be scattered or clustered in a frog-spawn pattern on the vulvar region. Lesions may be asymptomatic or associated with pruritus, burning sensations, serous fluid leakage, or secondary infections. Histopathologically, AVL is characterized by dilated lymphatic channels lined with flat endothelial cells. Additional features include varying degrees of papillomatous changes in the epidermis, hyperkeratosis, acanthosis, and erosion. Immunohistochemistry staining with lymphatic markers such as D2-40 can help to confirm the nature of the vessels as being of lymphatic origin.4Treatment is challenging because of the high recurrence rate, with an overall recurrence rate of approximately 43% after initial treatment.1Surgical excision is the most common treatment, with postsurgical recurrence rates of 23.1% to 25%; complete excision of skin, including lymphatic cisterns in subcutaneous tissue, may prevent recurrence.5,6Other treatments include sclerotherapy, laser therapy, cryotherapy, electrocautery, radiotherapy, or photodynamic therapy.2The present patient was referred to the gynecology department for surgical resection of the vulvar lesions; however, the procedure was postponed due to the sudden onset of acute lower extremity lymphangitis. Molluscum contagiosum, caused by the molluscum contagiosum virus, is clinically characterized by asymptomatic, small, shiny, dome-shaped papules with central umbilication. These lesions are usually asymptomatic or present with pruritus or pain. Histopathological examination reveals nests of eccrine ducts and tadpolelike structures embedded in fibrous stroma.8Condylomata acuminata, or genital warts, is a common sexually transmitted infection caused by the human papillomavirus. Immunohistochemical staining was positive for D2-40 in endothelial cells (Figure 2). A diagnosis of acquired vulvar lymphangioma (AVL) was made. AVL, also known as acquired lymphangiectasia of the vulva, is a rare, benign condition associated with architectural disruption, obstruction, and further dilation of previously normal lymphatic channels. It can occur secondary to cancers, trauma, radiotherapy, surgery, infections, and inflammatory diseases.1,2Cervical carcinoma, especially cervical squamous cell carcinoma, is the most common AVL-associated cancer.3Clinically, AVL presents as skin-colored papules or translucent, reddish vesicles, which may be scattered or clustered in a frog-spawn pattern on the vulvar region. Lesions may be asymptomatic or associated with pruritus, burning sensations, serous fluid leakage, or secondary infections. Histopathologically, AVL is characterized by dilated lymphatic channels lined with flat endothelial cells. Additional features include varying degrees of papillomatous changes in the epidermis, hyperkeratosis, acanthosis, and erosion. Immunohistochemistry staining with lymphatic markers such as D2-40 can help to confirm the nature of the vessels as being of lymphatic origin.4Treatment is challenging because of the high recurrence rate, with an overall recurrence rate of approximately 43% after initial treatment.1Surgical excision is the most common treatment, with postsurgical recurrence rates of 23.1% to 25%; complete excision of skin, including lymphatic cisterns in subcutaneous tissue, may prevent recurrence.5,6Other treatments include sclerotherapy, laser therapy, cryotherapy, electrocautery, radiotherapy, or photodynamic therapy.2The present patient was referred to the gynecology department for surgical resection of the vulvar lesions; however, the procedure was postponed due to the sudden onset of acute lower extremity lymphangitis. Although the condition improved after anti-inflammatory therapy, the patient refused further treatment and was lost to follow-up. Differential diagnoses in the present case include syringoma, molluscum contagiosum, and condyloma acuminatum. Molluscum contagiosum, caused by the molluscum contagiosum virus, is clinically characterized by asymptomatic, small, shiny, dome-shaped papules with central umbilication. Large cells with granular, eosinophilic, intracytoplasmic molluscum bodies are a typical histopathological feature.7Vulvar syringomas are benign adnexal tumors typically characterized by multiple small, firm, skin-colored to light brown papules scattered on the labia majora. These lesions are usually asymptomatic or present with pruritus or pain. Histopathological examination reveals nests of eccrine ducts and tadpolelike structures embedded in fibrous stroma.8Condylomata acuminata, or genital warts, is a common sexually transmitted infection caused by the human papillomavirus. Lesions may manifest in various forms, including smooth, flat, keratotic papules or exophytic cauliflowerlike masses. Koilocytic change is a helpful histopathological feature of condylomata acuminata and serves as a critical clue for differential diagnosis.9 This patient’s presentation illustrates findings typical of AVL, an uncommon complication from patients with a history of cervical cancer, radiation therapy, or surgical intervention. AVL should be considered in the differential diagnosis when papular or vesicular lesions develop in the vulvar region.
